3967.exq_: There are various possibilities, but typically, the first element bears less stress than the second and does not show the full array of tonal distinctions found on its last syllable
3967.tone: Five lexical tones. Peterson 2010 fn. 1 (opened, pp. 81-82): 'The orthography conflates representation of the Khumi tonal system (five underlying distinctions) and representation of the vowel system' — low checked, high checked, low falling, high falling, rising-falling. Peterson 2013 excerpt (gbq9): 'Khumi has five lexical tones, as well as about seven other tones resulting from the lexical tones' occurrence in particular morphosyntactic contexts'. Peterson 2019 excerpt: 'Syllables have an underlying tone'; sesquisyllabic half-syllables are written without a vowel and transcribed with a reduced vowel (p'liwng4 [pə1liwŋ4] 'heart'), i.e. the major syllable is the tone-bearing one, but the source is not seen calling this stress. The single stress statement is the compound one quoted; Peterson 2010 p. 85 describes the same left-member reduction purely in tonal terms ('the lefthand base of a compound in Khumi differs phonologically from an independent use of that base in not having the full range of possible tonal variation on its final syllable', e.g. tuuy 'water' low falling > low level in tuydueéng 'water gourd') without using the word stress. Grierson 1904 Khami sketch: 'at least two tones, the light and the heavy one', nothing on accent. No word-level stress placement rule found in any reachable text or excerpt.

tn.quote: Mro Khimi has two contrastive tones, H and L. Like Mara, there are no rising tones, and falling tones only occur phrase-finally. Mro Khimi has four tone melodies on the roots, L H LH and HL, toneless affixes, tone on suffixes spreading from roots, and polar tone on prefixes. ... Nasalized vowels and oral vowels are the only Tone Bearing Units (TBUs) in Mro Khimi. ... Since Mro Khimi does not permit contour tones, the final tones in words with more tones than syllables, such as the final L in /kʰøHL/ ‘country’, are left floating, resulting in [kʰǿ].

3968.prule: Khalilova 2009 (Kwantlada/Inkhokwari): stress on the final syllable when it is closed (CVC), otherwise on the penultimate syllable ('heavy syllables attract the stress'); examples at 2, 3 and 4 syllables (háq'u, rekéne, xuxut'ári vs ezól, raLád); stress is phonemic (ís-o 'say-IMP' vs isó 'that.GEN1'). tn.translation: 3. The system of syllable tones is standard: H, L, F, R. Secondary features of the tones: H - tense, loud; L - lax, quiet; F - sharp, short; R - drawn out in an open non-final syllable, short elsewhere. In disyllabic words the scheme HL predominates, but there are other schemes too: kožu/HL 'fang', soro/LH 'horse', ... The combinations RF, FR, FF, HF, LF are absent. 3970.dq: El acento en la lengua kickapoo se presenta en la antepenúltima sílaba de la palabra. [p. 58] ... Otro signo demarcativo afonemático positivo es el acento, el cual se encuentra fijo en la antepenúltima sílaba de la palabra y aunque el acento no marca el límite de la palabra, su posición indica la cercanía de él. [p. 95]

3970.prule: Accent is automatic (non-distinctive, delimitative; 'fonético') and fixed on the antepenultimate syllable of the word ('fijo en la antepenúltima sílaba de la palabra', p. 95; schema 'sss / (s)'sss / (ss)'sss / (sss)'sss / (ssss)'sss, p. 58), counted in the author's phonological syllables. A phonemic long vowel /V: is one syllable and is skipped like any other (['kuh.kuu.sa] /kuhku:sa/ 'puerco', [a'pe.nuu.ha] /apenu:ha/ 'niño', [ah'pa.pii.NI] /ahpapi:ni/ 'silla', [a'tuh.puu.NI] /atuhpu:ni/ 'mesa', [e'teh.tee.ki] /etehte:ki/ 'fruta'), while a phonetically long penult that carries the accent is analysed as two identical short vowels = two moras/two phonological syllables with the accent on the first ([a'naa.kwa] /anaakwa/ 'estrella', [me'saa.(w)I] /mesaawi/ 'grande', [meh'tee.(h)A] /mehteeha/ 'arco'); the author states that the accent position itself decides which analysis a VV sequence receives (p. 71). No weight condition is stated: closed penults (['me.6ih.kwa] 'granizo') and long-vowel penults alike are skipped. Disyllables: every transcribed phonetic disyllable (21 distinct forms) is initially accented (['ẽ.hẽ], ['wii.na], ['maa.ne], ['nii.na], ['yuu.we]); there is no explicit disyllable statement.
3970.srule: Only in imperative words: a secondary accent (acute) falls on the word-final syllable after the antepenultimate primary accent (['pîa.nú] 'ven', ['pîe.sú] 'dámelo', [ne'paa.nú] 'duérmete'; p. 59, forms again p. 71). 3970.tone: Moctezuma (Coahuila variety) describes no pitch or tone contrast: vowel length is the only distinctive prosodeme and the accent is non-distinctive ('El prosodema que tiene función distintiva en el idioma kickapoo es la cantidad vocálica', p. 93; 'el acento en el idioma kickapoo es considerado fonético en este análisis', p. 94). For the Oklahoma/Kansas variety Voorhis 1982 (pp. 83-84; consulted again) describes level vs falling pitch on long vowels: 'They are usually only realized as actual falling pitch when they happen to coincide with the sentence accent in a certain way. When they occur in a sentence later than the sentence accent, they are level, but their presence is indicated by the position of the accent: it is attracted toward the end of the sentence' (p. 84), with the merger of original clusters and long vowels 'in that part of a word which is beyond reach of sentence accent, namely, earlier than the third syllable from the last' (p. 84). Gathercole 1983 (IJAL 49:72-76, paywalled, not opened) calls this a tonal system. Moctezuma p. 99 reports Voorhis 1974 p. 8 minimal pair poohkamáaki 'duraznos' vs poohkámaaki 'en un durazno'; p. 100 reports putting the pair to Coahuila speakers, who denied any difference: '[ puuh.ka'maa.ki] / pu:hkamaaki / para ambos, afirmando la inexistencia de la palabra [ puuh'ka.maa.ki]'. So for the Coahuila variety the author holds the accent non-contrastive; a pitch-accent reading applies, if at all, only to the US variety.

3971.prule: Two-pattern (N-type) pitch accent, mora-counted from the right edge, no stress: every noun belongs to series α or β. α (kernelless, 'word-tone'): the bunsetsu (noun + particles) is the accent unit and only its penultimate mora is low. β: a rising kernel on the penultimate mora (−2) of the word; pitch rises there and stays high to the end of the bunsetsu in connective form, with a fall on the bunsetsu-final mora in citation form (the fall is intonational, not lexical). Intensity/stress is never mentioned.

3971.exq_: No stress rule, so no exceptions to one. Restrictions the source states on the pitch-accent classes: "ただし，1 拍語は α 系列の 1 種類のみである" (p. 51); "長母音をもつ形がすべて α 系列というわけではなく，[wi]:（桶），[na]:（中）などの β 系列もある" (p. 52); abstract p. 75: "a moraic nasal can bear a final high pitch of the word-tone, but not an ascend…
3971.tone: Entirely pitch-based description: a 二型アクセント (two-pattern accent) of the Kagoshima/Nagasaki N-type, mora (拍) as the counting unit, α = kernelless word-tone spread over the bunsetsu with only its penultimate mora low, β = 昇り核 (ascending kernel) on the word's penultimate mora, counted from the right edge; the two series are lexical classes (data in (7)–(8), pp. 52). Uwano calls α 無核型 and treats the β fall as intonation. Supporting sources in the copy consulted agree: Kubozono 2011 (NINJAL Kikai report, p. 51, p. 2) restates Wan as a 2型アクセント体系 with α bunsetsu-domain (次末拍のみ低く) and β word-domain (語の次末拍の前でピッチが上がる), mora-based; Uwano 2016 (Onseikenkyu 20(3), pp. 95, 97) revises the central/southern dialects to three-pattern after a γ series (rising kernel on the antepenultimate mora, −3, 3+-mora words only) turned up in loans and place names, and reconfirms northern Onotsu as three-pattern with length and special-mora constraints. No source mentions stress or intensity.

tn.translation: Noun patterns are listed in (7). However long the accent unit, there are only two oppositions: a 'two-pattern accent'. I name the series α/β ... The α series is the same at word and bunsetsu level (a word is a bare bunsetsu): 'the bunsetsu is the accent unit and only its penultimate mora is lowered'. The β series needs word-level specification: 'an ascending kernel on the word's penultimate mora (−2)'. Pitch goes high at the kernel mora, staying high to the bunsetsu end in the connective form but falling on the bunsetsu-final mora in the conclusive form. ... Against β, α counts as kernelless.

3972.dq: Generally, the lexical roots of Kilen are stressed on the first syllable ... A secondary stress will be involved when a word contains four syllables or more (p. 41); Compounds often form one phonological word and thus have just one stress (Aikhenvald, 2007). In Kilen, compounds are stressed on the first syllable of the first element; there is no second stress in the whole compound word (p. 52).

3973.prule: CONFLICT. (a) Geurtjens 1933, the N.B. heading his comparative wordlists of seven languages bordering Marind (Kaladdar and Teri-Kalwa = the two Kimaghama dialects, plus Koneraw, Komelom, Jab/Bibikem, Jei, Digul): 'The main stress always falls on the last syllable, unless this is a toneless ending, which is indicated by placing the sign ˘ on the vowel. From the last syllable the secondary stress skips forward [leftward] trochaically. In Digul the stress often falls on the penultimate.' = fixed final stress (penult when the final vowel is a breve-marked 'toneless ending'). (b) Drabbe 1949, the only descriptive primary (Glottolog's sole reference, fieldwork with Kimaghama-village speakers): no rule; he marks the stressed syllable with a grave accent 'when we think it necessary' and explicitly declines to say what kind of accent the language has; on wordlist p. 14 the marks fall on the initial syllable in most items (jèndjé, tùakwo, àvujö, mùndaé, tjàkra, èvendi, gònda, tjàma, dàdu, àmata, màku, wàmanda, pùrikwo), on the final in several (pörè, tjetjirè, uì, nöè, durò) and medially in one (kodàmbörö). (c) Voorhoeve 1975 (secondary, explicitly built on Drabbe's notes): 'stress, the occurrence of which seems unpredictable', potentially phonemic, no minimal pairs recorded. (a) is irreconcilable with (b)-(c) for the same words (Drabbe tùakwo, màku, tjàkra, dàdu, àmata, tjàma initial vs. Geurtjens' rule final).

Given the iambic rhythm of these languages, not only must non-phrase-final syllables be light, but phrase-final syllables (syntactic heads) must maintain a certain gravity.' 3974.heavy: Not applicable as a stress rule. Ratliff's 'light and heavy' = short/long, reduced/full syllables in a descriptive iambic-rhythm statement (reduced syllables: 'weaker stress and shorter duration than the following full syllables'), not a weight-to-stress assignment.
3974.prule: No word-stress rule is stated for Kim Mun. It is a lexical-tone language (eight tones in both the Lao and the Vietnam variety, Clark 2008; six tones in Savina 1926). The only stress-bearing statement is Ratliff's comparative inference that Mien and Mun share an iambic light/heavy prosody: minor (reduced) syllables and nominal prefixes are unstressed, short and toneless, and the following full syllable (phrase-final = syntactic head) is heavy; the explicit 'weaker stress... strong iambic rhythm' wording is Downer's about Iu Mien, and the Mun-specific primary evidence behind it (Shintani & Yang 1990: viii, quoted in Ratliff 2007) is a remark that 'in plurisyllabic words or contexts, a tonal and vowel neutralization is often observed', not a stress statement.

3984.tone: The source's own term is 'pitch accent' (p. 234 main text). Accent = high pitch on a short syllable; on long vowels a two-way contrast, high falling (accent on first mora, táaro 'star') vs low rising (accent on second mora, baál 'child'); p. 244 fn. 17: 'v́v (accent on the second mora) in most cases results from secondary lengthening following the reduction of ancient consonant clusters' (tapta- > tatta > taáto 'hot'), while an OIA long vowel gives accent on the first mora. Baart c.2003 (secondary, DIR-external, citing Schmidt & Kohistani 1998: 125-134): 'the underlying forms of the words have no tone at all... stress applies to the mora. Stress is assigned to one of the moras of the word', and a rule links H tone to the stressed mora. So: culminative, lexically placed mora-stress with a tonal realisation; no stress-position rule computable from syllable count or weight.

3990.heavy: Heavy = 'гласные исконно среднего или нижнего подъема' (e, o, ȯ, a, u < *o̭, ɯ < *ȯ̭; p. 252 adds i < *ḙ), i.e. the 'более звучные' (more sonorous) vowels; light = 'гласные исконно верхнего подъема' (i < *i, u < *u, ө < *i̮), the 'слабосонорные' vowels, with ө behaving as high although phonetically mid today. Weight is vowel height/sonority as fixed at the Proto-Komi stage, so surface u, i, ɯ are heavy or light word by word (etymologically); vowel length, codas and onsets play no role. Itkonen 1955: 28-29 uses the same split in Wiedemann's terms «schwer»/«leicht» (reflexes of Proto-Permic u, i̮, i light, all others heavy).

3991.tone: The source is a dedicated 90-page tone study (two level tones H/L, rising contour on monosyllables, tone-bearing nasals, three strata of tone rules, downstep, intonation; instrumental appendix on downstep). The words 'stress', 'prominence', 'intensity' and 'loudness' never occur in the tone paper, the 1992 MA thesis or its 2011 SIL re-edition; 'accent' occurs only as 'acute accent' (H-tone diacritic, p. 76) and 'circumflex accent' (footnote 10, foot of p. 81 between the 'page 81' and 'page 82' headers: a diacritic for a branching vowel). 'penultimate' hits concern an unpredictable H in a noun (footnote 8, pp. 80-81) and a falling contour on the penultimate syllable of declarative-final possessives (p. 143, after examples (114)-(117): 'Thus, regardless of dialect, a falling contour is obtained on the penultimate syllable when in the declarative-final position'), not stress. The 2011 re-edition defers tone to the 1992 paper ('A paper on tone has been presented in Thomas 1992'). 3992.prule: Main stress on the final syllable unless that syllable is a 'toonlooze uitgang', i.e. ends in the toonlooze (schwa-like, 'nauw hoorbare') e written ĕ; such a final syllable is skipped and stress falls on the penult. 3994.prule: Lexical tone, Manding type: every word carries one of two basic word-level tone schemes (H or L, realised over the whole word, e.g. Konya bá 'goat', bà 'mother', mɔ́ɔ̀ 'person', bàlà 'xylophone'); Konya's classes are the mirror image of Maninka-Mori's ('tonal inversion'). No word-stress rule is stated for Konya; at family level Vydrin says stress is absent in most Mande languages.

3994.tone: Two-way lexical tone classes on the word (H vs L; disyllabic HL vs LL), inverted relative to Maninka-Mori (Davydov p. 170). The only stress statement is family-level (Vydrin p. 34): stress is absent in most Mande languages, and where identifiable (Bamana, as 'foot stress') its functional load is small. tn.translation: Most Manding idioms have two basic word tone schemes. Thus in Maninka-Mori words with high and with low (rising) tone are distinguished. The tone schemes of monosyllabic and polysyllabic words coincide. ... [table Maninka-Mori/Konya: L / H 'goat' bà / bá; H / L 'mother' bá / bà; LL / HL 'person' mɔ̀ɔ́ / mɔ́ɔ̀; HH / LL 'xylophone' bálá / bàlà] As the table shows, high-toned words of Maninka-Mori correspond in Konya to words with low tone, and Maninka-Mori words having low tone correspond in Konya to words with high tone. ... the tones of Konya are inverted compared with Maninka-Mori.
